title: Onboard clients like a firm that has its act together
summary: A complete, buildable AI system for client intake and onboarding: turn intake forms into structured profiles, prepare kickoffs, collect documents, and generate a personalized onboarding plan.
audience: Consultants, agencies, professional-services firms, coaches, and small teams responsible for client onboarding.
learningPaths: Prepare the kickoff from approved facts
Build and approve the onboarding plan
assumptions: A responsible human owns the client relationship
Sensitive records use approved access-controlled systems
limitations: AI drafts can misstate scope or expectations
Legal, financial, privacy, and regulated onboarding requires qualified review
editorialIntro: The first two weeks decide how a client judges everything after. This playbook collapses the hours between "client signed" and "client feels taken care of" — intake to structured profile, kickoff prep, a welcome sequence, document collection, and a personalized onboarding plan. A person still approves every client-facing word.

editorialSections.title: The handoff after "yes" is where good firms quietly lose ground

blocks.text: A client signs. Then momentum stalls. Someone has to send the welcome email, collect documents and logins, schedule the kickoff, write up notes, and turn a signed proposal into an actual plan of work. For agencies, consultants, bookkeepers and accountants, coaches, and the many firms doing legal-adjacent work without being law firms, this is where things go wrong.

The intake questionnaire comes back half-filled and lives in an inbox. The kickoff runs long because nobody had time to prep. Assets trickle in over three weeks of reminders. Expectations get set on a call, then remembered differently a month later. None of this is a talent problem. Onboarding is repetitive, detail-heavy work that always competes with billable delivery, and delivery wins.

AI does not fix this by replacing the relationship. It reads the intake form into a structured profile, drafts the welcome sequence, preps the kickoff, and generates a personalized onboarding plan you edit rather than write from scratch. The client experiences a firm that is organized — because now you are.

editorialSections.title: A calm start protects revenue, referrals, and reputation

blocks.text: The onboarding window sets the tone a client uses to judge everything afterward. A confident, organized first two weeks builds trust that survives the rough patch later. A chaotic start — missed logins, an improvised kickoff, an expectation nobody wrote down — plants doubt that resurfaces months later as slow payment, scope arguments, or a quiet non-renewal. You rarely get a second chance to feel dependable.

The economics are concrete. If assembling a profile, prepping a kickoff, and writing an onboarding plan takes three or four hours of senior time per client done well, that work gets rushed or skipped exactly when you are busiest winning clients. Compress it to thirty minutes reviewing AI-drafted material and the standard holds even in your worst week. Every client should get the good version, not just the ones who signed during a slow month.

There is a retention dividend too. Clients who feel oriented and clear about what happens next ask fewer anxious questions, escalate less, and refer more. Onboarding is not overhead. It is the first delivery you make, and the one that decides whether the client believes the rest of your promises.

editorialSections.title: Service businesses that sell expertise and repeat the same handoff

items: The solo consultant or fractional operator. You do the selling and the delivery, so onboarding gets crammed into the gap between calls. You want a profile, a kickoff brief, and a plan generated from the intake form so you show up prepared instead of scrambling.

The small agency (2–20 people). You have an intake process, but it lives in one person's head and varies by who runs it. You want a repeatable system that produces a consistent, high-quality start regardless of who is on point that week.

Accountants, bookkeepers, and legal-adjacent firms. Your onboarding involves sensitive documents, engagement scope, and precise expectations, so structure and a clear record matter. Standardize intake and paperwork collection while keeping a human on every judgment call.
Coaches and boutique practices. The relationship is the product, and a warm, personalized welcome is part of the value. Let AI handle the assembly so your attention goes to the human part.

Not a fit: anyone hoping to fully automate client-facing onboarding with no human review. The point is to remove the busywork, not the person. Send everything unsupervised and you have automated away the trust you were building.

editorialSections.title: From a signed proposal to a client who feels taken care of

blocks.text: By the end of a build, you have a repeatable onboarding loop that runs the same way for every new client:

items: Intake. One well-designed form captures the facts you need once, so you never ask the same question twice across three emails.
Structured profile. AI reads the raw intake answers into a clean, consistent profile — goals, scope, stakeholders, constraints, and open questions — that any teammate can pick up.
Kickoff prep. A kickoff brief and draft agenda generated from the profile, so whoever runs the call walks in informed rather than reading the form live.
Welcome sequence. Drafted onboarding messages — welcome, what-happens-next, document requests, kickoff confirmation — in your voice, for a human to approve and send.
Document and asset collection. A trackable checklist of what you need, with requests drafted and receipts logged so nothing sits half-collected.
Personalized onboarding plan. A tailored two-to-four-week plan with milestones, owners, and expectation-setting that you edit and share, turning a signed scope into a visible path.

blocks.text: Every client-facing message and the final plan pass through a person before the client sees them. The AI does the assembly and drafting; you keep the judgment, the tone, and the accountability.

blocks.text: You do not need all of these. The manual version needs one AI chat tool, a form, and a document to hold the profile. Prices below are current as of mid-2026 and change often — confirm before you buy.
AI assistant required

ChatGPT Plus or Claude Pro, both about $20/month, for turning intake answers into a profile, prepping the kickoff, and drafting the welcome sequence and onboarding plan. Free tiers are fine for testing; paid tiers give you stronger models and higher limits once this is a real part of your week.
An intake form

Typeform, Tally, or Google Forms to capture client answers in one structured place. Google Forms and Tally have genuinely usable free tiers; Typeform is more polished but paid. Whatever you pick, the value is one clean set of fields feeding everything downstream.
A home for the profile and plan

Notion is a common choice — the Business tier runs about $20/user/month, and AI is now bundled into that tier rather than sold as the old separate add-on that was removed. Google Docs plus a spreadsheet works perfectly well too and costs nothing extra.
Document collection and e-sign

A storage or e-sign tool to gather sensitive files and engagement paperwork — a shared drive folder, or a light e-sign product for the engagement letter. Keep client documents somewhere access-controlled, not scattered across email attachments.
Automation glue optional

Zapier or Make to move a form submission into your profile doc and kick off the drafts. Zapier's Professional plan starts around $19.99/month annual for 750 tasks; a multi-step Zap burns one task per step per run, so budget by steps, not runs.
Guardrail note

You will handle client personal and business information, so treat data handling seriously: access controls, retention limits, and care about what you paste into AI tools. This is educational, not legal advice — see the risks section before you wire anything to sensitive documents.

editorialSections.title: Manual, semi-automated, fully implemented

blocks.text: Same loop, three levels of build. Start at the left even if you plan to end at the right — running onboarding by hand teaches you what a good profile and plan actually contain, and that judgment is what you encode later.
One form, one AI chat, one profile document

Build a single intake form and send it the moment a client signs. Paste the answers into your assistant to get a structured profile, prep the kickoff, draft the welcome sequence in your voice, and generate the plan. Read every word before it goes out.
Honest expectation: the first client is slow, because you are still deciding what "good" looks like. That time is the tuition you pay to build the automated version well.
The form and AI assemble; you review at two gates

The intake form feeds a profile automatically and the AI drafts everything. You keep two checkpoints: verify the profile against the raw answers (gate one), then read, edit, and approve each client-facing message and the plan before anything sends (gate two).
Where most service businesses should live for a good while: fast enough to be consistent across every client, slow enough to stay warm and correct.
A triggered loop with a mandatory approval gate

A signed proposal or submitted intake form kicks off the loop. It assembles the profile, drafts the welcome sequence, checklist, kickoff brief, and plan, and sets up a secure collection folder — then lands the package in a "Needs review" view. Nothing reaches the client until you flip the status to Approved.
"Fully implemented" does not mean "onboards clients by itself." It means everything except the judgment and the human warmth is automated.

Reality check: the full build has real maintenance. Intake forms change, prompts need re-tuning as your services evolve, and a broken Zap fails silently the week you are too busy to notice. Budget a few hours a month, and never remove the approval gate to "save time." A client who receives a hallucinated commitment because a bot sent it unsupervised is a client you have damaged. Automate the assembly, never the accountability.

editorialSections.title: From zero to the semi-automated loop

items: Design the intake form. List every question you currently ask across scattered emails and calls, then group them into one form: goals and success criteria, scope and deliverables, key contacts and decision-makers, deadlines, existing assets, access and logins needed, and service-specific fields. Keep it as short as it can be while capturing what you actually use.

Build the profile template. Create a document or Notion template with fixed sections: Client & contacts, Goals & success criteria, Scope & out-of-scope, Constraints & risks, Assets received, Open questions, and Onboarding status (Intake sent / Profile ready / Kickoff done / Plan shared / Onboarded). A consistent shape is what makes the system repeatable.

Save the prompts. Keep the four prompts below somewhere reusable, dated, and easy to paste. Treat them as version-controlled: when an onboarding goes unusually smoothly or badly, update the relevant prompt to encode what you learned.

Run one client fully by hand. Take your next real client through the whole manual loop — intake, profile, kickoff brief, welcome sequence, plan. Note every place the AI got something wrong or you rewrote heavily. Those notes are your tuning list.

Generate and verify the profile. Run the completed intake through the profile prompt. Read the result against the raw answers line by line. Confirm the model did not invent scope, deadlines, or commitments the client never made. Answer the open questions before moving on.

Draft the sequence and plan with your voice. Paste two or three real onboarding emails you have sent as a voice sample, then run the welcome-sequence and onboarding-plan prompts from the verified profile. Edit until it sounds like your firm, not a tool.

Approve, send, and collect. Read every client-facing draft, send the welcome sequence, and set up the document checklist and a secure folder. Log what arrives. Share the plan so expectations are written down.

Add automation last. Once the manual loop is smooth and the prompts are tuned, wire the repetitive moves — form submission creates the profile, AI drafts the package into a review view — in Zapier or Make, keeping the approval gate as a hard stop. Automate what you have validated, never the judgment or the tone.

editorialSections.title: Copy these, then make them yours

blocks.text: Intake to structured profile

You are helping me turn a new client's intake answers into a clean, structured client profile for my service business. My business: [what you do, in one sentence] The service this client bought: [engagement type / scope] Raw intake answers: [paste the client's completed intake form responses] Produce a profile with these labeled sections: 1. Client & key contacts (names, roles, decision-maker) 2. Goals & success criteria (what "done well" looks like) 3. Scope & explicit out-of-scope 4. Constraints, deadlines, and risks 5. Assets/access provided vs. still needed 6. Open questions — anything the intake did not answer or answered ambiguously, phrased so I can ask the client. Only use facts present in the answers. Do NOT invent scope, deadlines, or commitments. If something is unclear, put it in Open questions rather than guessing.
Kickoff brief generator

Using the client profile below, write a one-page kickoff brief and a draft agenda for a 45-minute kickoff call. Client profile: [paste the verified profile] Produce: 1. A 4-6 line summary someone could read right before the call to sound fully prepared. 2. The three most important things to confirm or align on. 3. A time-boxed agenda (intros, goals, scope confirmation, logistics, next steps). 4. 3-5 smart questions to ask, based on the open questions and any risks in the profile. Keep it practical and specific to this client. Do not add generic filler. Flag anything in the profile that looks unresolved before the call.
Personalized onboarding-plan generator

Create a personalized onboarding plan for this client covering the first [2-4] weeks. Client profile: [paste the verified profile] My standard onboarding steps (adapt these): [paste your usual steps, or leave blank to have them proposed] Produce a week-by-week plan with, for each item: - The action, the owner (me / client / shared), and the due point relative to kickoff. - A short milestone or check-in at the end of each week. - An "expectations" note per week: what the client should expect from us and what we need from them. Only commit to things supported by the scope in the profile. If the plan implies work outside the stated scope, flag it instead of including it. Keep the tone warm and clear.
Welcome / onboarding sequence (optional)

Draft a short onboarding message sequence for this client. My voice — match this tone exactly: [paste 2-3 real onboarding emails I've sent] Client profile: [paste the verified profile] Write four short messages: 1. Welcome + what happens next. 2. Document & access request (list exactly what we need, based only on the profile's "still needed" items). 3. Kickoff confirmation with the agenda highlights. 4. A day-3 check-in offering help. Rules: no fake urgency, no filler, no commitments beyond the scope in the profile. If a needed detail is missing, tell me what to fill in rather than inventing it.

editorialSections.title: Where this goes wrong, and how to catch it

blocks.text: Hallucinated commitments

The most dangerous failure mode: the model writes a deadline, deliverable, or promise the client never agreed to, and it looks confident enough to send. The prompts forbid inventing scope, and your approval gate is where you verify every commitment against the signed agreement before a client sees it.
Client data handling and PII

Intake forms and onboarding documents contain personal and sensitive business information. Store it with access controls and a retention limit, be deliberate about what you paste into AI tools and which tools you trust, and check whether your provider's terms and your client agreements allow it. Do not route confidential documents through automations you have not vetted.
Legal, financial, and compliance limits

Engagement scope, data-protection rules, and industry-specific obligations constrain how you collect, store, and act on client information. This playbook is educational, not legal, medical, or financial advice; RN Collins is a JD candidate, not a licensed attorney. Get qualified counsel for your jurisdiction and industry before relying on any of this for regulated work.
Over-automation losing the human touch

Onboarding is where the relationship is built. If a client receives a sequence that is obviously bot-assembled and unsupervised, you have automated away the exact warmth you were selling. Keep a person on the tone, and personalize beyond the template.
Garbage intake in, confident junk out
A half-filled or misread form produces a wrong profile that poisons everything downstream. Verify the profile against the raw answers, and resolve open questions before drafting.
Review cadence

Read every client-facing message before it sends during onboarding, review the profile against source answers for each new client, and audit your intake form and prompts quarterly against where onboarding actually snagged.

title: One asset, a week of content — still in your voice
summary: Turn one webinar, podcast, talk, or long article into a week of derivative content without losing the creator's voice or fabricating claims.
audience: Founders, experts, creators, consultants, and lean marketing teams repurposing long-form source material.
learningPaths: Complete a human voice and accuracy review
methodology: Ground every derivative in the source
Compare drafts with the voice guide
assumptions: The creator or editor performs final review
limitations: Repurposing does not create original authority
Transcripts and model drafts can omit nuance or misattribute language
editorialIntro: You already made the hard thing: the webinar, the podcast episode, the long essay, the recorded talk. This turns that one asset into a week of LinkedIn posts, a newsletter, short-form video scripts, and threads that still sound like you and never claim something you did not actually say. AI does the drafting; a voice guide and a fact-preservation rule keep it honest; you do the final edit.

editorialSections.title: You make one good thing, then it disappears

blocks.text: You spent weeks on a webinar. Two hundred people saw it live, a few dozen watched the replay, and then it went quiet. The insight is still good — but it is trapped in a sixty-minute recording nobody has time to rewatch. The same fate meets your best podcast episodes, your longest and most careful blog posts, and the talk you gave at that conference. You built assets with a long shelf life and then let them expire in a week.

The obvious fix is to chop each asset into many smaller pieces for the channels where your audience actually is. The problem is that doing this by hand is grinding work. Pulling the quotable moments, rewriting them for LinkedIn versus a newsletter versus a thirty-second video, and matching each to the platform's format takes hours per source — hours that never make the calendar, because the next webinar is already being planned.

AI closes that gap. But it introduces two new dangers that most people ignore: the drafts come out sounding like generic AI content, and they quietly invent statistics, quotes, and claims you never made. This playbook exists to get the speed without either of those failures.

editorialSections.title: Repetition builds a reputation; one-shot content builds nothing

blocks.text: Nobody remembers a single post. People remember a person who shows up saying consistent, useful things over and over, in the places they already scroll. Repurposing is how one hour of real thinking becomes ten touchpoints — and ten touchpoints is how a stranger starts to recognize your name.

The arithmetic is what makes it worth systematizing. If turning a webinar into a full week of channel content takes you six hours by hand, you will do it maybe once and then quietly stop. Compress the drafting to twenty minutes of review over AI output, keep an hour for real human editing, and the same asset now yields eight to twelve finished pieces at a quality you would sign. That is the difference between a content habit and a content wish.

There is a quieter benefit too. When you repurpose from a real source you actually created, every derivative piece is grounded in something you genuinely believe and said out loud. That is the opposite of the empty, everywhere-at-once content that makes audiences tune out — and it is why the fact-preservation rule below is not a nicety but the whole engine.

editorialSections.title: People who create long things and want them to travel

items: The founder or expert who publishes. You write essays, host a podcast, or give talks, and you know each one should become a dozen posts — but the repurposing never happens because you are busy making the next big thing.
The solo marketer or small team. You are responsible for a content calendar with no staff to feed it. One strong source per week, well repurposed, can fill most of it.

The consultant or coach with recorded calls and talks. Your best material is already spoken and captured. You want it working for you on LinkedIn and in a newsletter, in your voice, without hiring a ghostwriter.
Not a fit: anyone who wants a bot to autopost AI slop with no human review, or who has no genuine source asset to repurpose from. This playbook amplifies real thinking, not the appearance of it.

editorialSections.title: From one source to a channel-ready set, in your voice

blocks.text: By the end of a build, you have a repeatable loop that runs each time you publish something long:

items: Capture a clean transcript of the source asset, so the AI works from your actual words, not a summary of them.
Extract a voice guide once, from writing you have already published, so every draft is measured against how you actually sound.
Mine the transcript for atomic ideas — the standalone points, stories, and quotable lines worth their own piece.
Repurpose each idea per channel — LinkedIn post, newsletter section, short-form video script, X thread, quote-graphic caption, SEO snippet — under a rule that forbids inventing facts.
Generate hook and headline variants so you can pick the strongest opening rather than settling for the first.
Edit every piece by hand before it publishes, because the human pass is where voice and truth are protected.

blocks.text: The AI does the ninety percent that is transcribing, mining, and drafting. You keep the ten percent that is judgment: does this sound like me, and is every claim in it true?

editorialSections.title: Pick a tier and start; you can grow into more

ChatGPT Plus or Claude Pro, both about $20/month, for mining transcripts, drafting per channel, and generating hook variants. The paid tiers give you the stronger models and the longer context you will want when feeding in a full hour-long transcript.

A transcription tool to turn the audio or video into text. Otter and Descript are common; many podcast hosts and video platforms now include built-in transcripts, and Descript doubles as an editor if you also want to cut short-form clips. Accuracy on names and jargon varies, so always proofread.
A place to keep drafts

Notion is a natural home — one page per source, with the transcript, voice guide, and each channel's drafts together. Notion's AI features are bundled into the Business plan (about $20/user/month); the older standalone $10 AI add-on has been removed. A plain Google Doc works fine to start.
Scheduling / publishing

Buffer or Hypefury to queue and space out posts across channels, or each platform's native scheduler if you prefer to stay in-app. Scheduling is optional for the manual version — you can just post by hand — but it is what makes a weekly cadence stick.
Automation glue optional

Zapier to move a finished transcript into your drafting workspace and route approved pieces to your scheduler. Zapier's Professional plan starts around $19.99/month annual for 750 tasks; a multi-step Zap burns one task per step per run, so budget by steps, not runs.
Honest limits

None of this removes the editing. AI repurposing is a strong first-draft engine, not a publish button. Budget real human time on every piece — that is where the voice stays yours and the facts stay true. See the risks section before you automate anything.

editorialSections.title: Manual, semi-automated, fully implemented

blocks.text: Same loop, three levels of build. Start at the left even if you plan to end at the right — doing it by hand teaches you what "sounds like me" and "provably true" actually look like, and that judgment is what you encode later.
One transcript, one AI chat, one focused afternoon

Build your voice guide once from published work. Get a clean transcript. Mine it for atomic ideas, run the per-channel prompt that forbids inventing facts, then edit every draft against your voice guide and verify every claim before you post.
Honest expectation: the first pass is slow, maybe an afternoon for one source. That is the tuition you pay to build the automated version well.
The tools transcribe and draft; you review at two gates

Store your voice guide once. Auto-transcribe each source and proofread names and jargon. The AI batch-mines and batch-drafts. Then a fact-check pass (gate one) and a voice-and-send pass (gate two) before anything queues.
Where most creators should live for a while: fast enough to be consistent, slow enough to stay unmistakably yours.
A scheduled loop with a mandatory editing gate

A new transcript or episode triggers the loop in Zapier or Make. It cleans the transcript, attaches your voice guide and fact-preservation rule, drafts per channel plus hooks into a "Needs review" view, and pings you. Nothing publishes until you edit and approve.
"Fully implemented" does not mean "posts by itself." It means everything except the judgment is automated.

Reality check: this is a real build with real maintenance — transcription mishears names, models drift toward generic phrasing, and a broken Zap fails silently. Budget a few hours a month, and never remove the editing gate to "save time." The gate is where your voice and credibility are protected. An unedited AI post that invents a statistic will cost you more trust than the whole system saves you in hours.

editorialSections.title: From zero to the semi-automated loop

items: Extract your voice guide. Run the voice-guide prompt over three or four published pieces. Save the result in a doc titled "Voice Guide" and treat it as living: revise it when your writing shifts or when a draft sounds off despite following it.

Set up your source workspace. Create a template — a Notion page or doc — with sections for Transcript, Atomic ideas, LinkedIn, Newsletter, Video scripts, Thread, Captions, SEO snippets, and Status (Draft / Fact-checked / Edited / Scheduled / Published).

Transcribe and clean. Transcribe your source asset and read the whole thing once, fixing wrong names, terms, and mishears. This is the single most important quality step — every downstream piece inherits these words.
Mine atomic ideas. Run the idea-extractor prompt over the cleaned transcript. Review the list, keep the ideas that stand on their own, and star the two or three strongest to lead with.

Draft per channel. For each starred idea, run the per-channel prompt with your voice guide attached and the fact-preservation rule in force. Generate one piece per channel you actually use — do not spread yourself across platforms you will not maintain.
Generate hook variants. Run the hook-and-headline prompt on your lead pieces to produce several openings each. Pick the strongest by hand; a good hook is the difference between a read and a scroll.
Fact-check and edit. With the transcript open, verify every quote, number, and claim in every draft, then edit each piece into your voice. Cut generic phrasing on sight. Only then mark it Edited.

Add automation last. Once the manual loop is smooth, wire the repetitive moves (transcript in → mine → draft → review view → scheduler) in Zapier or Make, keeping the editing gate as a hard stop. Automate what you have validated, never the judgment.

blocks.text: Voice guide from your own writing

Below are 3-4 pieces I have actually written and published: [paste your writing samples] Study them and produce a reusable "voice guide" I can attach to future drafting tasks. Include: 1. Tone in 3-5 adjectives, with a one-line reason for each. 2. Sentence rhythm and length patterns you notice. 3. Words and phrases I clearly favor. 4. Words, cliches, and patterns I clearly avoid. 5. How I open and how I close. 6. A short "do NOT sound like this" list of generic phrasings that would break the voice. Base every point ONLY on the samples. Do not invent traits I did not demonstrate. Output as a labeled list I can paste later.
Transcript to atomic ideas

Below is a transcript of something I created: [paste transcript] Extract the standalone ideas worth their own piece of content. For each, output: - A one-line summary of the idea. - The type: insight / story / framework / quotable line / data point. - The exact wording from the transcript it came from (verbatim), with a rough location marker. Rules: - Only use what is actually in the transcript. Do not add ideas, examples, or claims that are not present. - For quotable lines and data points, quote them EXACTLY. If a number or claim is ambiguous in the transcript, flag it rather than cleaning it up. Return a numbered list, strongest ideas first.
Per-channel repurposing (fact-preservation rule)

Repurpose ONE idea into content for the channel I name. My voice guide: [paste voice guide] The source idea and its exact transcript wording: [paste one idea + verbatim source] Channel: [LinkedIn post | newsletter section | 30-sec video script | X thread | quote-graphic caption | SEO snippet] Hard rules: - Use ONLY facts, numbers, quotes, and examples present in the source above. Do NOT invent statistics, studies, quotes, names, or outcomes. If a claim would strengthen the piece but is not in the source, leave it out and tell me what I would need to add. - Match my voice guide. Avoid generic AI phrasing. - Format natively for the channel (length, line breaks, hook). Output the piece, then a one-line "claims used" note listing every factual claim and where in the source it came from.
Hook and headline variants

Here is a finished piece: [paste the draft] My voice guide: [paste voice guide] Write 6 alternative opening hooks (or headlines) for it. Vary the angle: curiosity, a concrete number from the piece, a contrarian take, a direct question, a short story open, a plain-value open. Rules: - Every hook must be true to the piece — no bait the content does not deliver, no invented stats. - Keep my voice. No "unlock", "game-changer", or hollow hype. Number them and mark the one you think is strongest, with a reason.

editorialSections.title: Where this goes wrong, and how to catch it

blocks.text: Fabricated stats and quotes

The single biggest failure mode: the model invents a statistic, a study, or a quote you never said to make a piece punchier. The prompts forbid invention and require a "claims used" trace, and your editing gate is where you verify every claim against the transcript before publishing.
AI-tell and sameness

Even truthful drafts can come out sounding like everyone else's AI content — the same rhythms, the same empty transitions. The fixes are the voice guide, a ruthless human edit, and cutting any line that could have been written about anything.
Copyright and attribution

Repurposing your own work is simple. Repurposing someone else's talk, article, or podcast is not — quoting, clipping, and reframing others' material raises copyright and attribution questions. When in doubt, attribute clearly, quote sparingly, and get permission; do not pass another person's ideas off as your own.
Platform authenticity

Audiences and platforms increasingly penalize content that reads as automated or inauthentic. Post as a human who reviewed the work, keep a real cadence rather than a firehose, and do not disguise AI-assisted drafts as spontaneous.
Legal, medical, financial guardrail

This playbook is educational, not legal, medical, or financial advice. RN Collins is a JD candidate, not a licensed attorney. For copyright, contracts, or regulated-industry content, get qualified counsel for your jurisdiction and situation.
Review cadence
Read a sample of published pieces weekly for voice drift, re-check your fact-preservation discipline monthly, and revisit your voice guide quarterly as your writing evolves.

title: The AI policy that makes everything else defensible
summary: Stand up a minimum viable internal AI policy with approved and prohibited uses, data-handling rules, human review, an audit trail, disclosure norms, and a review cadence.
audience: Small organizations formalizing AI use without a dedicated compliance function.
methodology: Review exceptions and update the policy
limitations: This educational playbook is not legal advice
A starter policy does not replace security, privacy, employment, or regulatory review
editorialIntro: Your team is already using AI — you just cannot see how. This is the trust layer underneath every other playbook: the minimum viable internal policy a small team can actually keep. A one-page use policy, a clear line between approved and prohibited uses, data-handling rules, a human-review gate before anything reaches a client or regulator, and an audit trail you can maintain without a compliance department. Enough structure to protect you, light enough that people follow it. Educational, not legal advice.

editorialSections.title: Your team is already using AI; you just cannot see how

blocks.text: Here is the uncomfortable truth about most small businesses in 2026: AI adoption already happened, and nobody signed off on it. Someone in accounts pastes a client contract into a free chatbot to summarize the tricky clause. A junior staffer drops a spreadsheet of customer emails into a consumer tool to draft a mailer. A contractor runs a patient intake note or a candidate's résumé through whatever app they had open. None of it is malicious. All of it is invisible to you.

This is shadow AI: real work getting done through unsanctioned tools, on unknown terms, with sensitive data you are contractually and sometimes legally responsible for. The moment client PII, a signed NDA, source code, or a trade secret lands in a consumer tool's input box, you may have created a disclosure you cannot take back — and you will not know it happened until a client asks how their data is handled and you have no answer.

Governance is not about slowing your team down. It makes the AI use that is already happening visible, safe, and defensible — so you can say yes to more of it with a straight face, instead of pretending it is not going on.

editorialSections.title: Trust is the thing you are actually selling

blocks.text: Every other AI playbook — lead generation, client deliverables, operations — assumes you can put AI output in front of a client without embarrassing yourself or breaching an agreement. Governance is what makes that assumption true. It is the layer underneath everything else, and skipping it does not make you faster; it makes you exposed.

Start with your contracts. Many client agreements, especially in professional services, healthcare, and finance, include confidentiality and data-handling terms written before anyone imagined a staffer pasting the deliverable into a public model. A clear internal policy — sanctioned tools only, no client data in consumer tiers, a review gate before anything ships — is often the difference between honoring those terms and quietly breaching them.

Then there is risk reduction that pays for itself. A single leaked dataset or a fabricated figure that reaches a regulator can cost more than a year of careful process. Governance lowers the odds and, just as importantly, gives you a record showing you took reasonable care — which matters enormously when something does go wrong.

The counterintuitive part: good governance enables adoption, it does not block it. When people know exactly which tools are safe and where the guardrails are, they stop hiding their AI use and start doing more of it openly. A policy that says "here is how to use AI well" gets far more real work done than a nervous, unwritten "please be careful."

editorialSections.title: Small teams handling other people's trust

items: The owner-operator (1–20 people). You have no legal or compliance staff, but you have clients who assume you are handling their information responsibly. You want the smallest policy that actually protects you, not a fifty-page document nobody opens.

The professional-services firm. Agencies, consultancies, bookkeepers, clinics, boutique law-adjacent and advisory shops — anyone whose contracts include confidentiality terms and whose reputation rests on discretion.

The team already deep into AI. You leaned into AI for real output and now realize you never wrote down the rules. This is the retrofit: getting the guardrails in place before an incident forces the issue.

Not a fit: large enterprises with existing compliance functions and legal teams — you need something heavier and jurisdiction-specific. And this is not a substitute for qualified counsel in regulated industries; it is a starting point that helps you have a smarter conversation with the professionals you do hire.

editorialSections.title: From invisible risk to a written, followable standard

blocks.text: By the end of a build, you have a lightweight governance system that a small team can actually maintain:

items: A one-page AI use policy in plain language, so every person on the team applies the same standard instead of their own judgment call.
An approved-and-prohibited list: named uses that are fine, named uses that are banned, and a simple path for classifying anything in between.
Data-handling rules everyone can recite: never paste client PII, secrets, or confidential material into consumer tools, and a short list of sanctioned tools cleared for real work.
A mandatory human-review gate for anything that goes to a client, a regulator, or the public — nothing AI-assisted ships without a named person checking it.
An audit trail that records what AI produced, who reviewed it, and when, so you can reconstruct any decision later.
Disclosure norms and a review cadence so the policy stays honest with clients and keeps up with a fast-moving field.

blocks.text: Crucially, none of this is a tool you buy. It is people and process, lightly supported by a shared document and a simple log. The AI can help you draft and triage; the judgment, the enforcement, and the ownership stay human.

editorialSections.title: Mostly a document and a log, not a purchase

blocks.text: Governance is people plus process, not software. The core of this playbook is a shared doc and a simple log. Prices below are current as of mid-2026 and change often — and tool terms change even faster, so verify current terms before you rely on them.
Shared policy document required

Notion, Google Docs, or any shared doc your whole team can reach. This holds the one-page policy, the approved/prohibited list, and the data-handling rules. Free tiers are fine. The requirement is not the tool — it is that the policy is written down, findable, and versioned.
Audit log required

A Google Sheet or a Notion database with one row per client-facing AI-assisted output: what was produced, which tool, who reviewed it, when, and the outcome. That is the entire audit trail. Do not over-engineer it; a log people actually fill in beats a perfect one they abandon.
Sanctioned AI tools

Enterprise and team tiers generally keep your inputs out of model training by default — ChatGPT Team/Enterprise and Claude Team, for example — while consumer free tiers may not. Team seats commonly run in the low tens of dollars per user per month, but pricing and, more importantly, the data-handling terms change; confirm the current terms in writing before you treat any tool as sanctioned.
Tool sanctioning process

Sanctioning is a decision, not a download. Before a tool goes on the approved list, someone checks: does it train on our inputs, where is data stored, does it meet our contracts? Keep a short list of cleared tools and a "not approved" list, and revisit both when terms change.
Team communication optional

Slack, Teams, or email for the review-gate ping and incident reporting — whatever your team already uses. The point is a clear, fast channel to flag "this needs review" and "I think something leaked."
Honest limits

No tool makes you governed. Software can hold the policy and the log, but enforcement, review, and ownership are human work. Anyone selling you a "governance platform" as a substitute for that work is selling you theater — and this is not legal advice; see the risks section.

editorialSections.title: Manual, semi-automated, fully implemented

blocks.text: Same policy, three levels of build. Start at the left even if you plan to end at the right — writing it by hand forces the decisions that matter, and that judgment is what you encode later. Governance cannot be automated away; the "fully implemented" version automates the paperwork, never the judgment.
One page in a doc, written this afternoon

Draft the one-pager with the policy prompt below: approved uses, prohibited uses, data rules, the review gate. Name your sanctioned tools. Put the one data rule in bold at the top. Start the log by hand for the next few client-facing outputs.
Honest expectation: the first draft takes an afternoon and feels awkward. That awkwardness is the tuition — a standard you can point to beats good intentions nobody can find.
The policy lives in a system; you hold the gate

Move the policy into a structured doc with version history, an owner, and a "last reviewed" date. Turn the log into a database with a form. Add a risk-triage step for new uses (green/yellow/red), then a human confirms. Wire the review gate into your workflow.
Where most small teams should settle: fast enough that governance is not a tax, structured enough that you can show your work if anyone asks.
An owned, enforced, regularly revisited standard

A named owner. An onboarding hook so every hire and contractor acknowledges the policy. A structured review gate — drafted, reviewed, approved, sent — that cannot be skipped. A living audit trail. A scheduled quarterly revisit. Disclosure norms baked in.
"Fully implemented" does not mean "runs itself." Governance is ongoing work — enforced, revisited, actually followed — or it is just a file.

Reality check: a policy nobody reads is theater — worse than nothing, because it creates false comfort. And to be clear, this playbook is educational and is not a substitute for qualified legal or compliance advice. RN Collins is a JD candidate, not a licensed attorney. For your specific jurisdiction, industry, and contracts, get qualified counsel. This gets you to a smarter starting point, not to compliance.

editorialSections.title: From zero to an owned, enforced policy

items: Draft the one-page policy. Run the policy prompt below, then rewrite the output in your own words. Put it in a shared doc titled "AI Use Policy," date it, and lead with the single data rule in bold. Keep it to one page — length kills adoption.

Define the approved and prohibited list. Name the approved uses (drafting internal notes, summarizing your own documents, brainstorming) and the prohibited ones (pasting client PII or secrets into unsanctioned tools, sending unreviewed AI output to clients or regulators). Anything not listed defaults to "ask first."

Set your data tiers. Sort information into a few tiers — public, internal, confidential/regulated — and state which tier is allowed in which tool. Confidential and regulated data goes only into sanctioned, terms-verified tools, if at all.

Define the human-review gate. Write the one-sentence rule: anything AI-assisted going to a client, regulator, or the public gets reviewed and signed off by a named person first. Decide who reviews, what "reviewed" means (facts checked, no leaked data, tone right), and where drafts wait.

Set up the audit-trail log. Create a sheet or database from the template below: date, item, tool, who produced it, who reviewed it, outcome, notes. Make logging faster than skipping it, and log every client-facing item from day one.

Train the team. Walk everyone through the policy in a short session — not an email they will not read. Cover the one data rule, the sanctioned tools, the review gate, and how to log. Have each person acknowledge they have read it.

Set the review cadence. Put a recurring hold on the calendar (quarterly works for most small teams) to re-verify tool terms, update the approved list, refresh the "last reviewed" date, and review any incidents. A cadence is what keeps the policy alive.

Appoint an owner. Name one accountable person for the whole thing. Without an owner, every other step slowly rots. The owner does not have to do all the work — they have to make sure it keeps happening.

blocks.text: Draft a one-page internal AI use policy

You are helping me draft a one-page internal AI use policy for a small business. This is a starting draft for me to edit, not final legal advice. My business: [type of business, e.g. a 6-person bookkeeping firm] The sensitive data we handle: [e.g. client financials, PII, contracts] Tools we want to sanction: [e.g. ChatGPT Team, Claude Team] Produce a one-page policy with four labeled sections: 1. Approved uses — 4-6 specific, allowed AI uses for our work. 2. Prohibited uses — 4-6 specific, banned uses (be explicit about never pasting client PII, secrets, or confidential material into tools not on our approved list). 3. Data rules — plain-language rules for what data may go into which tool, tied to sensitivity tiers. 4. Review gate — the rule that anything AI-assisted going to a client, regulator, or the public must be reviewed and signed off by a named person first. Keep it plain, short, and readable. Flag anywhere I should consult a qualified attorney for my jurisdiction, industry, or contracts.
Audit-log row template

Copy this header row into a spreadsheet or Notion database. One row per client-facing, AI-assisted output. Date | Item / deliverable | Tool used | Produced by | Reviewed by | Review date | Data sensitivity (public / internal / confidential) | Passed review? (Y/N) | Sent to | Notes / issues Example row: 2026-07-05 | Q2 client summary email | Claude Team | R. Okafor | J. Mensah | 2026-07-05 | Internal | Y | Client (Acme) | Reworded one figure; verified against source.
Use-case risk triage (green / yellow / red)

Classify a proposed AI use for my business as GREEN, YELLOW, or RED. This is a starting assessment for a human to confirm, not a final ruling. Our approved uses: [paste] Our prohibited uses: [paste] Our data sensitivity tiers: [paste] Proposed use: [describe: what someone wants to do, which tool, what data is involved, and where the output goes] Output: - Rating: GREEN (clearly approved), YELLOW (needs a human decision and possibly extra safeguards), or RED (prohibited or high-risk). - Reason: 2-3 sentences tied to a specific policy point or data tier. - If YELLOW: the exact questions a human should answer before deciding. - If RED: the specific rule or risk that makes it off-limits. Do not guess about tool terms or the law; flag where I need to verify current terms or consult qualified counsel.
Incident quick-write (optional)

Help me write a short, factual internal record of a possible AI-related data incident. No blame, just facts. What happened: [e.g. a contract was pasted into a consumer tool] When and who: [date, role — not for punishment, for the record] Data involved: [what kind, whose] Produce: a 4-6 sentence factual summary, a list of immediate steps to take, and a note on whether this may need to be escalated to qualified legal/compliance counsel. Do not offer legal conclusions.

editorialSections.title: Where this goes wrong, and how to catch it

blocks.text: This is not legal, compliance, medical, or financial advice

Read this twice. This playbook is educational. RN Collins is a JD candidate, not a licensed attorney, and nothing here creates an attorney–client relationship. You must get qualified counsel for your specific jurisdiction, industry, and contracts before relying on any policy you build from this — especially in regulated fields like healthcare, finance, and law.
Over-restriction kills adoption

A policy so strict that people cannot get real work done just pushes AI back into the shadows where you cannot see it. The goal is safe, visible use — not a ban dressed up as governance. If your rules are being ignored, they may be wrong, not your team.
An unenforced policy is theater

Writing the document is the easy part. If nobody reviews outputs, nobody logs, and nobody owns it, the policy creates false comfort and protects you less than an honest "we have no policy yet." Enforcement and ownership are the whole game.
Data leakage is the core danger

The failure you are guarding against is sensitive data landing in a tool that trains on it or stores it insecurely. Verify tool terms in writing, keep the one data rule front and center, and treat every consumer free tier as unsafe for confidential material until proven otherwise.
Regulatory and tool terms change
AI law and tool data-handling terms are moving fast. A policy that was correct last quarter can be stale now. This is exactly why the review cadence exists — a frozen policy quietly goes wrong.
Review cadence

Spot-check the audit log monthly for gaps, re-verify sanctioned-tool terms and refresh the approved list quarterly, and review any incidents and your disclosure norms with qualified counsel at least once a year or whenever your contracts or regulations change.

title: An internal brain your team can actually ask
summary: Turn scattered documents, messages, and tacit knowledge into a reliable internal knowledge system with grounded retrieval, citations, freshness controls, and access boundaries.
audience: Teams whose operational knowledge is fragmented across documents, messages, and individual employees.
assumptions: Document owners can identify authoritative versions
Users receive access only to information they are allowed to see
limitations: Retrieval cannot repair incomplete or contradictory source knowledge
Permissions and freshness require continuing maintenance
editorialIntro: Turn scattered docs, buried Slack threads, and the answers that live in one person's head into a knowledge base your team queries in plain language — one that quotes your own documents, cites where each answer came from, and admits when it does not know. No mystery answers. No pretending a search box is the same as knowing something is true.

editorialSections.title: The answer exists somewhere — nobody finds it in time

blocks.text: Every growing team runs up the same quiet debt. The onboarding steps live in a Google Doc someone wrote two roles ago. The real reason you switched vendors is in a Slack thread from March. The way you actually handle a refund sits in one person's head, and when they are on vacation the question just waits. The knowledge is not missing — it is scattered, undated, and unfindable at the exact moment someone needs it.

So the same questions get asked over and over in chat. New hires spend their first month interrupting senior people. Two teams do the same task two different ways because each found a different half-true doc. And when the one person who knows leaves, part of how the company works leaves with them.

AI does not fix this by generating more content. It fixes it by turning what you already have into something you can question in plain language — and, done right, by refusing to make things up when the answer genuinely is not written down. The hard part was never the model. It is deciding what counts as the truth, and keeping that truth current.

editorialSections.title: A findable answer is a decision made faster, the same way twice

blocks.text: When the right answer is one question away, the whole team moves differently. New hires get productive in weeks instead of quarters because they can ask instead of wait. Support and ops give consistent answers because everyone reads from the same source. And the senior people who used to be a human help desk get their focus back, because the routine questions no longer route through them.

The arithmetic is plain. If a recurring question costs someone ten minutes to track down, and it gets asked twenty times a week across the team, that is a few hours a week evaporating into a search you already paid to write down once. A knowledge base that answers in seconds does not just save the time — it stops the wrong answer from spreading when someone gives up and guesses.

There is a durability dividend too. Knowledge that lives only in conversation walks out the door with the person. Knowledge that is collected, structured, and queryable becomes an asset the company keeps — one that gets more valuable as it gets more complete, not less valuable as people turn over.

editorialSections.title: Teams whose knowledge outgrew the people holding it

items: The scaling small business or startup (5–100 people). You have crossed the size where everyone just knows how things work. Questions now get asked in three channels and answered three ways. You want one place people trust.
The operations or people lead. You own onboarding, process, and "how do we do X," and you are tired of being the search engine. You want new hires answering their own questions correctly by day two.
The support or customer-facing team. You need consistent, correct answers fast, and you need to know which policy or doc an answer came from so you can trust it before repeating it to a customer.

Not a fit: anyone hoping to point AI at a pile of contradictory, undated docs and get reliable answers without curating first. Garbage in is confident garbage out — the curation is the work, not the shortcut.

editorialSections.title: From scattered sources to a cited, current, plain-language answer

blocks.text: By the end of a build, you have a loop that keeps your internal brain honest and up to date:

items: Collect the real sources of truth — docs, wikis, key Slack decisions, the process a person carries in their head — into one inventory instead of five scattered homes.
Curate them: pick the one canonical version of each thing, mark the rest archived, and date what is current so the system never quotes a doc you retired.
Structure the content into clear, titled, single-topic pages so both a person and a model can find the right passage fast.
Ground answers strictly on those sources, so the assistant quotes what you wrote rather than inventing plausible-sounding filler.
Cite every answer back to the specific doc it came from, so anyone can verify before they act.
Maintain the source of truth on a cadence — because a knowledge base that stops being updated becomes a confident source of wrong answers.

blocks.text: The system's job is to retrieve and quote your knowledge, not to author it. The truth stays something humans own and keep current; the AI just makes it findable and readable.

editorialSections.title: Pick a tier and start; you can grow into more

blocks.text: You do not need all of these. The manual version needs one AI chat tool and the docs you already have. Prices below are current as of mid-2026 and change often — confirm before you buy.
AI assistant required

ChatGPT Plus or Claude Pro, both about $20/month. This is what you use to clean up messy docs, draft FAQs, and — in the manual version — answer questions from context you paste in. Free tiers work for testing; paid tiers give you the stronger models and higher limits you will want once this is real.
A doc hub with AI search

Notion is a common home for this. Notion Business runs about $20/user/month, and the AI features (Ask Notion / AI search across your workspace) are bundled into the Business tier now — the old separate ~$10 AI add-on has been removed. Custom Agents, if you build them, draw on metered credits (roughly $10 per 1,000 credits) on top of the seat price, so watch usage.
Alternative doc hubs

Google Drive works if your docs already live there. Purpose-built knowledge tools like Slab or Guru add cleaner structure, verification workflows, and freshness reminders — useful once your library grows past what a folder can manage.
A real RAG assistant advanced

To ground an assistant strictly on your own docs, you need a vector store to index your content plus an assistant or API layer that retrieves the relevant passages and answers only from them. This is developer-level effort — cost varies widely with volume and how much you build versus buy — and it is genuinely more work than turning on AI search. Do not start here.
Sync / automation glue optional

Zapier or Make to keep sources in sync — for example, pushing a resolved Slack decision into your doc hub. Zapier's Professional plan starts around $19.99/month annual for 750 tasks; a multi-step Zap burns one task per step per run, so budget by steps, not runs.
Guardrail note

Whatever you use, keep confidential and personal data inside an environment you control and check what your tools do with your content. Set permissions so the assistant surfaces only what a given person is allowed to see. This is not legal advice — see the risks section.

editorialSections.title: Manual, semi-automated, fully implemented

blocks.text: Same loop, three levels of build. Start at the left even if you plan to end at the right — doing it by hand teaches you which docs are actually canonical and how bad the contradictions are, and that judgment is what you encode later.
One AI chat, the docs you have, an afternoon

Inventory your top five to ten sources. Pick one truth per topic. Clean one messy doc into a FAQ, answer a real question grounded in it, and run the gap-finder to see what your docs cannot answer yet.
Honest expectation: the first pass is slow, and most of the time goes to deciding what is true. That is the tuition you pay to build the grounded version well.
A doc hub with AI search finds it; you keep it curated
Your cleaned, canonical pages live in a hub with built-in AI search, so anyone asks in plain language and gets an answer with a link back to the source. You keep two jobs: curation and freshness.
Where most teams should live for a long time: fast, cheap, and honest enough — without the real engineering of a custom RAG build until you need it.
A grounded RAG assistant, cited, permission-aware

A retrieval-augmented assistant indexes your docs, retrieves the passages relevant to each question, and answers only from them — quoting sources, respecting who is asking, and declining when the answer is not there.
"Fully implemented" is not a weekend project. It means real engineering plus ongoing curation, with the freshness routine treated as load-bearing.

Reality check: grounding reduces hallucination but does not eliminate it — and it does nothing for a stale source. If a document is out of date, the assistant will cite it and give a confident, wrong answer with a straight face. The maintenance that keeps your source of truth current is not overhead you can cut later; it is the load-bearing part of the whole system.

editorialSections.title: From scattered docs to a curated, AI-searchable hub

items: Inventory and pick the truth. List every source that answers a common question, note its owner and last-trusted date, and choose one canonical version per topic. Archive the losers so nothing can quote a doc you retired.

Clean each source into single-topic pages. Run the FAQ extractor to turn rambling docs into clear, titled, one-question-per-answer pages. A model retrieves a tight, well-titled passage far better than a wall of text.
Add owner and freshness fields. Give every page an owner and a "last reviewed" date. This is the discipline that keeps the source of truth true, and it is the field the whole system leans on.
Load into your doc hub. Put the curated pages into Notion or your chosen hub in a clear structure — by team or by topic — so both people and AI search can navigate it.

Turn on AI search and test it. Enable Ask / AI search across the workspace, then throw your team's real questions at it. Log every wrong answer; the fix is usually a content gap, not a settings tweak.
Run the gap-finder. Use the gap-finder prompt to list the questions your library cannot answer yet. Prioritize by how often each is asked, and write the missing pages.

Set permissions and a review cadence. Restrict pages so people see only what they should, and schedule owners to re-confirm or update their pages when review dates pass. Retire stale material on sight.

Consider a grounded RAG build only if you need it. If AI search over curated docs is not enough — you need strict citations, customer-facing reliability, or permission-aware retrieval at scale — scope a RAG assistant. Automate the parts you have already validated by hand; never automate away the curation.

editorialSections.title: Copy these, then make them yours

blocks.text: Doc-to-clean-FAQ extractor

You are cleaning up an internal document into a clear FAQ so my team and an AI search tool can both find answers fast. Here is the document: [paste the messy doc] Produce a set of Q&A pairs where: - Each question is one a real teammate would actually type. - Each answer is self-contained and uses ONLY facts stated in the document. Do not add best practices or outside knowledge. - If the document is ambiguous or contradicts itself, do not smooth it over — list the ambiguity under "Needs a human decision" instead of guessing. - Give each Q&A a short, descriptive title. End with a one-line note on anything that looks out of date.
Grounded-answer system prompt

You answer questions using ONLY the context documents provided below. Follow these rules exactly: 1. Base every answer solely on the provided context. Do not use outside or prior knowledge, even if you think you know it. 2. Cite the source: after each answer, name the specific document (and section, if given) the answer came from. 3. If the answer is not fully contained in the context, say exactly: "I don't know based on the current documents." Then say what document would need to exist to answer it. 4. If two documents disagree, say so and quote both — do not pick a winner on your own. 5. Never invent policies, numbers, names, or dates. Context documents: [retrieved passages go here] Question: [user question]
Knowledge-gap finder

Here is the full list of topics and pages currently in our internal knowledge base: [paste page titles, or a summary of what's covered] Here are the questions our team actually asks most often: [paste real questions from Slack/support/onboarding] Do two things: 1. List the questions that our current pages CANNOT fully answer, ranked by how often they seem to be asked. 2. For each gap, name the single page we should write to close it and who is the likely owner (a role, not a guess at a person). Do not invent answers to the gaps. Only identify what's missing.
Freshness reviewer (optional)

Review this internal page for signs it may be out of date: [paste page + its "last reviewed" date] Flag: references to old tools, people, prices, dates, or policies that may have changed; anything that contradicts a newer page I paste; and any claim that should have an owner re-confirm it. Do not rewrite the page — just list what a human should verify.

editorialSections.title: Where this goes wrong, and how to catch it

blocks.text: Hallucination when ungrounded

An assistant left to answer from general knowledge will invent plausible policies and numbers. Ground it strictly on your own documents, require citations, and make "I don't know" an acceptable, expected answer.
Stale sources, confident wrong answers

Grounding does not help if the grounded doc is out of date. A retired policy that stays in the index gets cited with total confidence. Every page needs an owner, a review date, and a way to fall out of the system when retired.
Confidential or personal data leaving your environment

Feeding sensitive docs or PII into a tool means trusting where that content goes. Check your tools' data handling, keep sensitive material in environments you control, and exclude what should not be indexed at all.
Access control and permissions
If the assistant can surface a document to anyone who asks, it becomes a leak. Retrieval must respect who is asking so people see only what they are allowed to see.
Over-reliance
A confident, cited answer can still be wrong if the source was wrong. Teach the team to click through to the source for anything consequential, rather than treating the assistant as an oracle.
Legal, medical, and financial limits

This playbook is educational, not legal, medical, or financial advice; RN Collins is a JD candidate, not a licensed attorney. Do not let an internal assistant stand in for qualified professional advice, and get counsel for your jurisdiction and industry on data and privacy obligations.
Review cadence
Spot-check answers weekly, have page owners re-confirm freshness on each page's schedule, and audit permissions and the gap list quarterly.

editorialIntro: A fit-first system that turns your ideal-client definition into a short list of real people worth talking to — enriched with genuine context and reached with a message you would be glad to receive. No scraped-then-blasted lists. No mail-merge pretending to be a relationship.

editorialSections.title: You need the right conversations, not more noise

blocks.text: Agencies, consultancies, fractional operators, boutique firms — they live or die by pipeline. But the two usual ways of building it both break. Referrals are wonderful and completely unpredictable; you cannot forecast a quarter on hope. Bought lists blasted through a cold-email tool feel efficient right up until your domain reputation tanks, your reply rate sits at half a percent, and the few replies you get are annoyed.

The real problem is not volume. It is that finding people who genuinely fit your offer, learning enough to say something true, and doing that every week is slow manual work — the kind that gets dropped the moment client work heats up. So pipeline arrives in feast-or-famine waves, and the famine always shows up at the worst time.

AI does not fix this by letting you send more. It fixes it by collapsing the hours between "here is my ideal client" and "here is a warm, specific first message to a person who matches" — so the work actually gets done, week after week, at a quality you would put your name on.

editorialSections.title: Consistency compounds; spikes evaporate

blocks.text: A predictable trickle of qualified conversations changes how you run everything else. You price with confidence instead of discounting out of fear. You turn down bad-fit work because another conversation is already booked. You plan hiring against a number you trust rather than a feeling.

The economics are stark. If sourcing and personalization take forty-five minutes per prospect done well, you will realistically touch a handful of people a week and then stop. Compress that to five minutes of review over an AI draft, and the same person reaches thirty or forty fitting prospects a week without lowering the bar. That is the difference between a channel that works and one that stays a good intention.

There is a reputational dividend too. Outreach that clearly understands the recipient earns replies even when the answer is "not now" — and "not now, but stay in touch" is a pipeline asset. Spray-and-pray earns spam complaints, which quietly poison every future email from that domain.

editorialSections.title: Owners and small teams who sell expertise

items: The founder-seller. You are the person who closes, and prospecting is what falls off the calendar first. You want a review-ready short list you can act on in a coffee break.
The small agency or consultancy (2–20 people). You have a clear ideal-client profile but no full-time SDR, and you want outreach that reads like a senior person wrote it, because one effectively did.
The fractional executive or specialist. Your market is narrow and named — a few hundred companies, not a few million — so precision beats volume every time, and generic lists are useless to you.
Not a fit: high-volume transactional B2C, or anyone hoping to send ten thousand identical emails a day. This is built for quality and defensibility, not blast radius.

Source companies and named contacts that match, from a real data provider rather than guesswork.
Enrich each one with genuine context — recent news, role, a plausible trigger — so there is something true to say.
Qualify against your disqualifiers so bad-fit names never reach the outreach step.
Draft a personalized first message and one follow-up, in your voice, that a human reviews before anything sends.
Track what happens so you learn which segments and angles actually convert.

items: Write and store the ICP. Run the ICP prompt. Paste the result into a doc titled "ICP + Disqualifiers" and treat it as version-controlled: date it, update it when a segment converts unusually well or badly.

Build the pipeline sheet. Columns: Company, Contact, Title, Link, Fit signals, Trigger, Disqualifier check, Draft message, Draft follow-up, Status (New / Reviewed / Approved / Sent / Replied / Meeting), Notes.

Export a starter batch. Pull 25 matches with available enrichment. Spot-check five rows by hand — is the data actually right? Bad inputs make confident, wrong drafts.

blocks.text: ICP + disqualifiers

You are helping me define an ideal client profile for my service business. My business: [what you do, in one sentence] My best past clients: [2-3 examples and why they were great] My worst-fit clients: [1-2 examples and what went wrong] Produce: 1. A tight ICP: industry, company size, revenue band, and the buyer role who signs off. 2. A "why now" trigger list: 4-6 observable signals that a company is likely ready for what I offer (e.g. new funding, a specific hire, a public initiative). 3. Hard disqualifiers: 4-6 signals that mean I should NOT reach out, even if other things match. Format as three labeled lists. Be specific and observable, not aspirational. Ask me one clarifying question if my inputs are thin.
Qualification pass

Here is my ICP and my hard disqualifiers: [paste ICP + disqualifiers] Below is a batch of prospects with enrichment data: [paste rows: company, title, headcount, notes] For each row, output: KEEP or CUT, and one short reason tied to a specific ICP criterion or disqualifier. If a row lacks the data to judge, mark NEEDS-CHECK rather than guessing. Do not invent facts about any company.
Personalized outreach draft

Write a first-touch email and one follow-up. About me / my offer: [one or two sentences] My voice — match this tone exactly: [paste 2-3 real emails you've sent] The prospect: Company: [name] Contact: [name, title] Genuine context I found: [the real trigger or detail] Rules: - Under 90 words for the first email. One clear, low-friction ask. - Open with the specific context, not "I hope this finds you well." - No flattery, no fake urgency, no "quick question" subject lines. - Only reference facts I gave you. If context is weak, say so and suggest what I should find before sending. - Follow-up: 2-3 sentences, adds a new angle, easy to ignore.
Reply triage (optional)
Classify this reply as: Interested / Not now / Not a fit / Referral / Unsubscribe. Then draft a two-sentence response that matches the category. Reply text: [paste]

editorialSections.title: Where this goes wrong, and how to catch it

blocks.text: Fabricated context
The biggest failure mode: the model invents a "recent funding round" that never happened. The prompts forbid invention, and your approval gate is where you verify claims before they embarrass you.
Deliverability collapse

Volume without warming, honest unsubscribes, and real personalization will burn your domain. Keep daily sends low, authenticate your domain (SPF/DKIM/DMARC), and never send cold at scale from your primary domain.

Anti-spam rules (such as CAN-SPAM in the US and similar regimes elsewhere), data-protection law, and platform terms all constrain what you may collect and send. This is educational, not legal advice; RN Collins is a JD candidate, not a licensed attorney. Get qualified counsel for your jurisdiction and industry.
Sameness at scale
If every message uses the same skeleton, personalization becomes theater. Review for variety, and rotate openings and angles.
Bad data in, confident junk out
Enrichment providers are often wrong. Spot-check, and treat every field as a claim to verify, not a fact.
Review cadence
Read a sample of sent messages weekly, revisit your ICP monthly against who actually replied, and audit disqualifier hits quarterly.

title: SOPs that run the business without you
summary: Use AI to capture, draft, standardize, test, and maintain standard operating procedures with roles, decision points, checklists, and accountable human review.

editorialIntro: Get the work out of your head and onto the page. AI drafts your Standard Operating Procedures from a walkthrough — clean steps, roles, and decision points — so the business runs when you are not in the room. The AI drafts fast; a human who owns the process verifies that every step is true before anyone follows it.

editorialSections.title: The business runs on knowledge only you have

blocks.text: In most owner-led businesses, the real operating manual lives in one person's head. You know the exact order to onboard a client, which supplier to call when the first one is out, how to close the books, what "done" looks like for a deliverable. None of it is written down, because writing it down is tedious and the work is always more urgent than documenting the work.

So the business is quietly hostage to your presence. A new hire takes months to get useful because you are their only reference. You cannot take a real vacation without your phone lighting up. Quality drifts depending on who happened to do the task and what they remembered. When someone leaves, a chunk of how the business actually works walks out the door with them.

AI does not fix this by writing generic templates you will never use. It fixes it by collapsing the hours between "I know how to do this" and "here is a clear, step-by-step SOP a competent person could follow" — so the documentation actually gets created, and stays created, instead of remaining a someday project.

editorialSections.title: Documented work is transferable work

blocks.text: A process that only exists in your memory cannot be delegated, audited, improved, or sold. A process written down as a good SOP can be handed to a new hire, checked against reality, refined when it breaks, and repeated at a consistent standard whether you are watching or on a plane. That is the whole difference between owning a job and owning a business.

The economics are plain. Writing a solid SOP by hand — thinking through every step, every role, every branch, then formatting it so someone can follow it — is a half-day of focused work per procedure, which is exactly why the backlog never shrinks. Feed a recorded walkthrough or a short interview into an AI assistant and you get a clean first draft in minutes. Your job shifts from author to editor: verifying, correcting, and filling the gaps the AI could not know. That is the difference between an SOP library that exists and one that stays a good intention.

There is a compounding benefit too. Once a process is written down, you can see it — and seeing it is the first step to improving it. Documented steps expose the redundant approval, the handoff that always stalls, the check nobody actually does. You cannot streamline what you have never made visible.

editorialSections.title: Owners and teams whose operations live in their heads

items: The owner who is the bottleneck. Everything routes through you because nothing is written down. You want a documented playbook so the team can act without asking, and you can step away without the wheels coming off.

The small team about to hire (2–30 people). You are bringing people on and re-explaining the same tasks over and over. You want onboarding that scales past your patience — SOPs a new hire can follow on day one.

The operations lead standardizing quality. The same task gets done three different ways depending on who does it. You want one documented standard, with the checklists and decision points that make the outcome consistent.

Not a fit: anyone hoping to publish AI-written procedures for safety-critical, regulated, or high-liability work without expert sign-off. This playbook speeds up the drafting; it never replaces the qualified human who owns the process and stakes their name on it.

editorialSections.title: From a walkthrough to a living, followable SOP

blocks.text: By the end of a build, you have a repeatable loop that turns tacit knowledge into documentation you actually maintain:

items: Capture a process by screen-recording yourself doing it, walking through it aloud, or interviewing the person who owns it — no blank page required.
Draft that raw capture into a structured SOP: purpose, prerequisites, numbered steps, decision points, and a roles table so everyone knows who does what.
Verify every step against reality, because the process owner — not the AI — is accountable for accuracy. This is the non-negotiable gate.
Standardize format, naming, and structure across every SOP so the library reads as one system, not a pile of documents.
Maintain each SOP with a documented owner and a review date, so it gets updated when the process changes instead of quietly going stale.
Convert finished SOPs into quick-reference checklists and onboarding guides, so the documentation becomes something people use daily, not a binder nobody opens.

blocks.text: A human who owns the process always verifies before an SOP is published. The AI does the ninety percent that is drafting and formatting; you keep the ten percent that is knowing whether it is actually true.
